text: evaluation. DOPER’s capabilities are robust; but in this study we focus on using the battery charging optimization to maximize revenue in response to an hourly price signal. Several assumptions are key in determining how the battery responds to a price signal. In this analysis, we assume (1) customers are allowed to export to the grid (2) prices are symmetrical, such that the cost of importing electricity in a given hour is equal to the revenue from exporting in that hour. Because of these assumptions, operation of behind-the-meter batteries is dependent only on the battery’s physical characteristics and the price signal; notably, price response is agnostic to customer loads, PV generation, or other electricity considerations at the site. Therefore, we are able to run a single optimization for each price profile of interest; the optimal dispatch resulting from that optimization will then be applicable to any battery energy storage system (BESS) responding to that price profile. The model aims to represent a common Li-ion battery. The key battery parameters assumed in the model are as follows: ● Duration of 4 hours, i.e., power capacity (kW) one fourth the energy capacity (kWh) ● Round-trip efficiency of 92%, modeled as 96% efficiency for charge and discharge ● Self-discharge of 3% per month, or approximately 0.004% per hour ● Minimum state of charge of 20% ● Battery degradation is not considered, as the 1-2 cycles/day expected for price response will not have substantial impact on the battery lifetime. Additionally, we assume an optimization window of one week, meaning that the hourly prices are known one week ahead of time. DOPER optimizes the charging and discharging in each hour of the year based on the state of the battery in that hour and the prices for the following week. The model is initiated by assuming a state of charge of 65% and requires that the battery ends the analysis period (in this case, one year) with that same state of charge. 2.3.4 Single-driver EV simulations This analysis supplements the EV load shifting modeling done using the “fully dispatchable load model” described in Section 2.3.2. The fully dispatchable load model considers EVs that can be 13 https://github.com/LBNL-ETA/DOPER 16 charged at any time, regardless of driving status or parking location. Further, the fully dispatchable load model uses the aggregate EV charging load shapes that were available in the Phase 4 DR study. In reality, EV drivers will face charging constraints (at a minimum, that they cannot charge while driving), and will have unique, “spiky” load profiles as opposed to the smoothed out average load shape used in the above analysis. Therefore, we analyzed individual driving profiles in order to determine the optimal charging behavior under different scenarios of driving behavior. While this analysis addresses some of the aforementioned limitations of the high-level analysis, it suffers from two key limitations: (1) we do not know the representative driving profiles for the entire state, and therefore cannot scale up our results to statewide totals and (2) the model focuses on optimal charging behavior and does not include default or baseline charging
